changes.summary: Reflecting the varied and eclectic intellectual inclinations of John and Dominique de Menil is a wide-ranging collection of art from the 4th to 18th centuries, originating in Europe and the parts of North Africa and Western Asia controlled by the Roman and later Byzantine Empires. These holdings include 1,375 works from the Medieval and Byzantine era (4th–mid 15th century) and more than 7,000 objects from the Early Modern era (late 15th–late 18th century), during which many of the characteristics of the modern world emerged, among them scientific inquiry, global exploration and colonization, humanism, and nation-states. The Menil’s collection of Byzantine, Post-Byzantine, and Russian icons is widely regarded by scholars as one of the most important in the United States. These holdings are displayed in a darkened, intimate space designed to evoke a chapel. The icon collection embodies the aesthetic and spiritual values that guided the de Menils throughout their lives as collectors. Rooms dedicated to the broader Medieval and Early Modern eras are presented adjacent to the icon gallery. On display are objects that illustrate the daily life of medieval Byzantium, featuring Byzantine church furnishings and a smaller collection of Western European works like reliquaries, architectural fragments, and religious statuary. Medieval art and artifacts are situated alongside noteworthy paintings, prints, sculpture, and decorative arts from the 15th to 18th century. Selections include significant paintings by or attributed to Christopher Amberger, François Clouet, Jean-Baptiste Greuze, Christian Luycks, François de Nomé, and Anthony van Dyck.
